svg.text: Inside a Sixfold cache: 4 KiB, 2-way set-associative, 32-byte lines, least-recently-used replacement
src/Instruction_Cache.sv and src/Data_Cache.sv have the same shape: 64 sets x 2 ways x 32 bytes. Example: a load from address 0x0000_2072.
which of the lines that share this set?
set 3 selects one row in every array, in the same cycle
all of this happens in one cycle:
On a miss: refill (MISS_LATENCY = 10, so a miss costs 11 cycles)
core stalls: FETCH1 holds its PC (I-cache) or the load waits in EXECUTE (D-cache)
an empty way first, otherwise the one LRU points at (chosen before this cycle's LRU update)
after a demand miss on line X, line X + 1 is fetched in the background if it is not present
D-cache is write-through, no-allocate: main memory always has the data, a cached copy is updated too
addresses 0x1000_0000 and up (putchar) bypass the cache entirely
Two arrays exactly 2 KiB apart share every set index. In a direct-mapped cache they evict
each other on every access ("thrashing"). With 2 ways both lines live in the same set.
Size cost of this cache, per line: 1 valid + 21 tag + 256 data bits; plus 1 LRU bit per set:
128 lines x 278 bits + 64 = 35,648 bits of storage for 32,768 bits of data (8.8% overhead).
Real CPUs: 32 to 64 KiB L1 caches with 8 to 12 ways and 64-byte lines, a 4 or 5 cycle load-to-use
latency (pipelined), and stride and stream prefetchers instead of just "next line".
